title: U.K. Sending Voyager Tanker To Help Defend Saudi Airspace
body: The Royal Air Force (RAF) is deploying one of its Voyager aerial refueling jets to help Saudi Arabia defend against ongoing attacks from the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels of Yemen. The decision marks the first publicly known international military assistance offered to Saudi Arabia specifically for its fight against the Houthis, which erupted over the summer. The move came hours before U.S. President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly meeting that he believes a peace deal with Iran will be reached after the U.S. midterm elections in November. The British action is significant because, while it involves just one tanker, other key Saudi allies have yet to heed the Kingdom’s request for military help specifically to battle the Houthis. Although it’s important to note some assets already deployed to defend against Iranian attacks could be helping with the Houthi threat now. A Royal Air Force Typhoon FGR4 accompanies a Voyager tanker during a Quick Reaction Alert training scenario in March 2026. (Crown Copyright) Crown Copyright Last week, Trump turned down a direct plea from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, to attack the Houthis. Meanwhile, Pakistan and Turkey, which signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia, have yet to provide any direct military aid. The pact holds that an attack on one is considered an attack on all; however, it doesn’t stipulate exactly what actions should be taken. Saudi Arabia, under repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks as well as suspected strikes from Iranian-backed militias in Iraq , is struggling to defend its oil infrastructure. The Kingdom is also facing a challenge supporting the anti-Houthi forces it backs in the Yemen civil war that reignited in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran that began Feb. 28 . At issue beyond protecting the Saudis is growing concern over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key chokepoint now largely controlled by the Houthis, who are preventing the Saudis from using it to ship oil. Earlier this year, the Houthis imposed a blockade on the Strait, and began striking Saudi ships in the southern part of the Red Sea as well as critical energy terminals on that body of water. Iranian proxies have also struck the vital East-West pipeline that feeds oil to be transferred and shipped via the Red Sea in order to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran vastly curtailed shipping after the launch of Operation Epic Fury. The pipeline reportedly reopened today after being shut down following a long-range drone attack. The Saudi Arabian East-West pipeline after it was damaged by an attack. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor) The stark reality is that if Saudi refineries are destroyed and the pipeline is shut down for months if not longer, the last major lifeline from the region, and especially to Europe, would be closed off, sparking a deeper energy crisis. Concern over these factors spurred Britain to act, the Ministry of Defense (MoD) noted. It said it was acting on a request from Saudi Arabia and that the jet would “support Saudi Arabia’s defensive operations in aid of the legitimate Yemeni government.” “Escalating tensions in the Gulf could have negative consequences here in the UK—such as rising prices, disruptions to energy supplies, and increased costs for British businesses,” the ministry explained. “The Houthis pose a threat to stability in the Middle East; therefore, it is in the UK’s national interest—economically and in terms of security—that they do not succeed in their aims.” “We unequivocally condemn Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and our position is clear: both Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have the right to self-defense,” the ministry added. The jet will operate from a U.K. air base in Cyprus and will begin air-to-air refueling operations in the coming days, the BBC reported. The MoD said the Voyager will fly only in support of missions to shoot down missiles and drones, though Saudi aircraft are also bombing Houthi ground positions in Yemen, in part to get at drone and missile launchers and storage sites. Houthi officials have accused the Saudis of killing civilians in some of these attacks . It should be noted that, more than a decade ago, the U.S. was supporting the Saudi coalition’s previous bombing campaign against the Houthis by providing aerial refueling and intelligence. However, then-Defense Secretary James Mattis ended that in 2018 during the first Trump presidency after growing concerns over the large number of civilian casualties . The Voyager can only refuel the Royal Saudi Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons, Panavia Tornados, and Italian Air Force Typhoons that have been in the Kingdom since before the fighting with the Houthis broke out, as well as any other similarly equipped allied aircraft. That’s because the tanker only has probe-and-drogue aerial refueling , not the boom required for gassing up other receptacle-equipped aircraft. You can read more about this in our story here . The view from the cockpit of an A400M during air-to-air refueling with a Voyager KC3 using its probe and drogue system, via the fuselage refueling unit. Crown Copyright The Voyager will not be the first British asset to be sent to help Saudi Arabia since the launch of Epic Fury. In March, the U.K. sent its Sky Sabre air defense system and troops to the Kingdom to help defend against attacks from Iran. The British Army Sky Sabre state-of-the-art intermediate air defence system. (Corporal Adam J Wakefield) Corporal Adam J Wakefield “This support builds upon the UK’s existing military contribution to Saudi air defense, which includes the deployment of an air defense system and British personnel to help protect against missile and drone attacks,” the MoD pointed out on Tuesday. “Saudi Arabia and Yemen are steadfast partners of the UK and play a vital role in regional stability. It is in the UK’s interest to safeguard regional stability, protect vital trade and energy supplies, and encourage a diplomatic resolution to the conflict in Yemen.” The civil war in Yemen erupted in 2014 and expanded a year later when a Saudi-led coalition joined forces with the government ousted by the Houthis. The fighting between Saudi-led forces and the Houthis largely abated after a tenuous ceasefire was signed in 2022. The Saudis held off on getting involved in the recent Red Sea conflict which saw the U.S. and coalition warships duking it out with the Houthis, and eventually led to a U.S.-led air campaign over Yemen. The United Kingdom was the other significant player in that air campaign. Tensions, as we noted earlier in this story, reignited in recent weeks after the Houthis joined the U.S.-Iran conflict on the side of their major supporter. On Tuesday, Houthi spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Sare’e claimed that Saudi Arabia conducted 19 airstrikes across rebel-held territory in Yemen that involved the latest round of civilian casualties . The Saudis have not directly responded. Brig. Gen. Yahya Sare’e. (Houthi Telegram) As we stated earlier in this story, hours after the U.K. announced it was sending a Voyager tanker to Saudi Arabia, Trump addressed the ongoing conflict with Iran during his speech to the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The American leader called for international isolation of Iran and repeated his stance that he was at an inflection point on deciding what course to take moving forward. The situation has settled into an uneasy pause interrupted by sporadic Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. It has been weeks since the U.S. last struck Iranian targets. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump asked rhetorically. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?” Trump added that he believes he will make a peace deal with Iran after the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, which could decide which party controls Congress. With gasoline and diesel price increases damaging the economy, the war and Trump’s handling of it have been very unpopular with voters . In a CNN and SSRS poll , released Tuesday, 64% of those responding said the U.S. is not winning the war in Iran , while 36% disagreed. In addition, 78% of participants said Trump is not doing enough to end the conflict with Iran and 22% said he was. Trump to the UN: "Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly? Do I drive them into hell?" pic.twitter.com/cIYBO1Mp3w — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 22, 2026 After a bilateral meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham following his UN speech, Trump claimed the Iranians still want to make a deal . “They want to talk to us,” he said. “They have been talking to us, even today they’ve been talking to us, and the relationship is developing. But we can’t let them – and they understand that – we can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.” A U.S. negotiating team, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with Iranian officials on the sidelines of Tuesday’s U.N. meeting. That sideline session lasted about three hours and went well, according to Trump, who offered no details on the discussions. Trump: US officials met with the Iranian delegation for three hours – "it was a good meeting" — Polymarket Intel (@PolymarketIntel) September 22, 2026 For their part, the Iranians said they are willing to negotiate, but on their terms. “A senior Iranian official said Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if the U.S. fulfilled Tehran’s demands to ease military pressure and lift an American blockade on Iranian ports,” Reuters reported . “The official added that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington via mediators last week.” Contact the author: howard@twz.com The post U.K. Sending Voyager Tanker To Help Defend Saudi Airspace appeared first on TWZ .

title: Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
body: A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation. The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan. The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran. “In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write. To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include: Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps. Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production. Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses. Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering Routing updates and briefings to Congress on these issues The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons. In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile. The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031. The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles. The Barracuda-500 cruise missile, built by Anduril. Courtesy of Anduril Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger , now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked. “It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said. The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued. Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability. “Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?” A U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon taxis on the flight line at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., carrying the Rusty Dagger, a Family of Affordable Mass Munition – Lugged weapon. (U.S. Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Thomas M. Barley) A Numbers Game The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait. But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior. “The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.” Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory. “China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said. And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.” “We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.” Airmen with the Air National Guard Air Force Reserve Command Test Center load a Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile on a pre-block F-16 for a test launch. (Air Force photo by Todd Cromar) Breaking a Stalemate The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm , now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell. “Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.” Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network. What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses. This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks. “Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.” Airmen inspect a live AGM-158C Long Range Anti-Ship Missile on a munitions trailer alongside a B-1B Lancer during a U.S. Air Force LRASM Event Zero at Dyess Air Force Base, Texas, June 2, 2026. (Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Caleb Schellenberg) “The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said. That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once. “I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said. Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything. “The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.” While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA. “That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said. For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM. “You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.” The post Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Air Power Is Key Counterterror Tool, but It Has Limits
body: A campaign of airstrikes in Somalia forced al-Shabaab to limit group communications and shift away from large gatherings of top leaders. In northwest Nigeria, an airstrike against Lakurawa terrorist camps forced fighters to flee to the north. Local sources told researcher Viktor Marsai that many of the terrorists were shocked at being targeted and had previously felt safe from airstrikes. “Neither example demonstrates a full defeat of terrorist groups, but these cases demonstrate how airstrikes can weaken groups’ coherence and operational capacities — at least for a time,” he wrote for The Soufan Center in an August 4 brief. Air power can have a significant counterterrorism impact, but experts say there are limits. They warn against sole reliance on air forces and encourage more coordination between air and ground forces. “Combating violent extremism in Africa requires a more comprehensive strategy; airstrikes eliminating training camps and high-value targets — including senior commanders — alone cannot obliterate terrorist groups,” Marsai wrote. In the Sahel, terrorist groups use irregular tactics to exploit weaknesses in security forces that adhere to traditional structures. Fatai Alli, a retired major general in the Nigerian Army, said that air and ground forces must integrate intelligence and restructure for better mobility. “Without ground forces to exploit the effects of air-delivered fires, insurgents simply disperse, regroup, and reconstitute,” he wrote in a February report for the Africa Center for Strategic Studies.“This reveals a deeper structural gap: ISR [intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance] assets, already insufficient in number, are not matched by the ground strike capability or the command-and-control architecture needed to act on intelligence at speed. Battlespace management remains slow and fragmented. It often takes hours for headquarters to gain awareness of an unfolding attack, during which time frontline units are left to fight alone with minimal reinforcement or resupply.” Operations in Somalia and the Lake Chad Basin have shown that airstrikes are more effective when targets are concentrated in a small area. Fighter jets, helicopters and drones deployed relatively close to battlefields that covered a few hundred square kilometers have had more impact than those in vast Sahel deserts. “In the Mali-Burkina Faso-Niger tri-border area, the Liptako Gourma region covers more than 500,000 square kilometers,” Marsai wrote. “Terrorist groups move relatively fast and freely on this vast terrain, launching attacks sometimes from a distance of hundreds of kilometers.” The Nigerian Air Force is aiming to modernize its fleet and foster better coordination with other service branches. In August, the NAF said it had increased its presence over Sokoto State to support joint security operations. Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, NAF director of public relations and information, said terrorists and bandits often exploit difficult terrain with mobility and concealment to evade ground forces. “By leveraging the reach, speed, flexibility and precision of air power, the NAF is better positioned to locate, disrupt and degrade hostile elements, deny them freedom of movement, and create opportunities for surface forces to consolidate gains,” he said in an August 24 statement. Air Marshal Sunday Aneke, chief of the air staff, added that asymmetric threats demand a responsive NAF to act on intelligence and coordinate quickly with ground troops. “Our objective is clear: to sustain pressure on criminal elements, deny them freedom of action, and create the conditions for our surface forces to dominate the operational environment,” he said. “We will continue to employ air power intelligently, professionally and decisively in synergy with sister services and other security agencies, while maintaining the highest regard for civilian safety.” Civilian casualties have been a major issue as the NAF has broadened its campaign of airstrikes against terrorists and bandits. Marsai warned that one of the biggest criticisms against the use of airstrikes is that they can cause collateral damage that can radicalize innocent civilians and strengthen terrorist groups’ propaganda and misinformation efforts. However, he believes that the evolving fight against terrorism necessitates the integration of air and ground forces. “While serving as an instrument in governments’ toolboxes, airpower can help shape effective counterterrorism strategies, but alone cannot destroy extremist organizations,” he wrote. The post Air Power Is Key Counterterror Tool, but It Has Limits appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Ukraine’s new interceptor drone moves toward mass production after first kills against jet-powered Russian drones that fly like cruise missiles
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukrainian drone manufacturer Wild Hornets says its new STING-family interceptor drone has destroyed about ten Russian Geran-4 jet drones and several Geran-5s—technically also drones but ones whose jet engines make them functionally small cruise missiles—in limited deployment over recent days, according to an interview with a company representative published by NV on 22 September. The company says it plans to begin mass production within about a month after completing combat tests. Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-powered Shahed-type drones this year. At least twenty firms were already racing to field interceptors by early September. Their higher speeds can cut the reaction time for Ukrainian mobile fire groups from about a minute to as little as six seconds. Two companies have completed combat tests, and 67 companies are working on interceptors, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . A new product, not an upgrade Wild Hornets told NV it began work on jet interception in early 2026 and described the new interceptor as an entirely new product rather than an upgrade of the existing STING design. To handle the faster targets, the company developed a remote-control system called Hornet Vision Ctrl that lets experienced pilots operate interceptors across multiple sectors at once—the same system now used against jet-powered Gerans. "We are working on that, but right now we are focused above all on creating a cheap, mass-producible, and simple-to-use means of countering jet Shaheds," the company told NV, answering a question about expectations that Russia could field mass jet missiles at 700–800 km/h by winter. The company said it knows of no fully automatic interception system proven in combat and that its own AI integration is aimed at assisting the operator. A schematic of Russia's jet-powered Geran-5 long-range attack drone. Russia is producing up to 500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, according to Ukrainian military intelligence. Credit: Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine's Defense Ministry. The jet-powered threat Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat said in August that the use of jet-powered drones had increased roughly fivefold in July compared with June. The Geran-5 can reach speeds of up to 600 km/h and carry a warhead of roughly 90 kg, according to specifications published on HUR's War & Sanctions website. The new jet Shaheds run on turbojets from a single Chinese company. Iran, which originally armed Russia with Shaheds, now wants the jet-powered Geran-5 remake back. Earlier this month, a new interceptor successfully hit a jet-powered Shahed during testing, but " some aspects of controlling the interceptor still need to be refined ," Zelenskyy said . Days later, he showed footage of a Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) interceptor destroying a jet-powered Shahed during a military counterintelligence operation. The SBU said it was the first footage showing the destruction of a jet-powered Shahed. Separately, footage published by Wild Hornets showed its STING interceptor striking a Geran-5—a jet-powered drone that functions as a small cruise missile—in flight: Another Geran-5 shot down by a STING S interceptor Thanks to the skill of the crew—in particular, the pilot with the call sign “Babay” from the 1020th Air Defense Regiment—the target was neutralized. The warhead of this model weighs up to 90 kg, and its range reaches 950 km. https://t.co/oMBz9PCbgs pic.twitter.com/vO1Dk8PoLm — Wild Hornets (@wilendhornets) September 21, 2026 Read also $16 bn or lives of Ukrainians: Kyiv is furious after EU took two of Russia’s richest men off its sanctions list Russia is spending jet-powered drones on Ukraine’s toilet-paper factory.
